catalog_quote: Comme dans la plupart des autres langues bantoues, l’accentuation joue un rôle secondaire en sso et n’est pas distinctive. Globalement on peut dire que c’est la première syllabe de la base qui se trouve légèrement accentuée par rapport aux autres syllabes. La longueur des consonnes dans la position de C1 de la base est généralement plus importante que celle des consonnes dans d’autres positions. L’accentuation se voit également par une pique d’intensité plus élevée sur la première syllabe que sur les syllabes successives (et le préfixe nominal s’il y en a). Ceci est illustré par le spectrogramme du mot ‘amour’, /ìdzìŋɡə̀/ dans la Figure 8. ... Figure 8 Spectrogramme du mot ‘amour’, avec en vert l’intensité, montrant qu’il y a une pique d’intensité sur la première syllabe du mot. ... 3.3.2 Hauteur mélodique. La hauteur mélodique a une fonction distinctive en sso, comme dans la quasi-totalité des langues bantoues. Il y a deux registres, haut et bas, ainsi que deux tons distinctifs, le ton haut (noté /H/) et le ton bas (noté /B/).

new_statements.translation: As in most other Bantu languages, stress plays a secondary role in Sso and is not distinctive. Overall one can say that it is the first syllable of the base [stem] that is slightly stressed relative to the other syllables. Consonant length in the C1 position of the base is generally greater than that of consonants in other positions. Stress is also visible as a higher intensity peak on the first syllable than on the following syllables (and than on the nominal prefix if there is one). This is illustrated by the spectrogram of the word 'love', /ìdzìŋɡə̀/, in Figure 8.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive weak prominence on the first syllable of the stem (base), i.e. the root-initial syllable; noun-class prefixes are not stressed. Cues: lengthened stem-initial consonant (C1) and an intensity peak on the stem-initial syllable. Tone (H vs L) is the distinctive suprasegmental; stress is secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the statement is hedged ('Globalement on peut dire', 'légèrement accentuée'). Yee 2022 (SIL) independently notes no penultimate lengthening and 'no data yet showing that stress plays an important role in Swo'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, stated over the morphological base (stem) vs. nominal prefix; evidence from citation forms (isolated words, spectrogram of a prefixed noun). Tonal language with two tones (H, L), sec. 3.3.2.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, So (Cameroon) [sox] soca1235 = Sso/Swo/Suə, Bantu A82, east of Akonolinga (Nyong-et-Mfoumou, Centre Region). Vermeir 2024 explicitly maps her 'sso/swo' to A82 / sox / soca1235 (Table p.13) and worked mainly in Mvansso, i.e. the sso-est (badjémé) dialect; Yee 2022 and the SIL orthographies cover the Melan and Emvane canton varieties. Not to be confused with So/Soo of Uganda (Kuliak) or Sô of DRC.

sources.note: sec. 2.0 Syllable Structure, p.4 (p.5): 'Prosodically, Bantu languages tend to exhibit penultimate stress with vowel lengthening.. Evidence in Swo for vowel lengthening in the penultimate syllable is not present. In fact, there is no data yet showing that stress plays an important role in Swo.' sec. 4.3 (p.17) speculates word-final /k/ > [ʔ] 'possibly because [it] is not stressed'. sec. 5.0 Tone: two level tones H, L; contours only on heavy syllables. No stress-placement statement.

sources.note: A talk on the interaction of relative-clause formation and tone in Swo; per the author's later thesis (a work listed here, sec. 3.3.2.5.4) the relativised noun, fronted, often receives a high tone of relativisation on its nominal prefix or on the first stem syllable when there is no prefix, in a two-tone (H, L) system — the talk is presumably the fuller treatment of this grammatical H tone.
